content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has outlined preferred product characteristics (PPCs) for monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) aimed at HIV prevention. These guidelines are designed to ensure that products are developed in a way that supports their optimal use globally, including in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The PPCs articulate the desired attributes of products for licensure, policy recommendations, and programmatic implementation in LMIC settings. They are based on criteria such as feasibility and addressing unmet medical needs in priority disease areas identified by WHO. The primary audience for these PPCs includes entities seeking WHO policy recommendations and prequalification for their products. It is important to note that these PPCs do not override existing WHO guidance and are subject to regular updates to reflect advancements in prevention, research, and development. The current PPCs focus on the preferred attributes of mAbs for HIV-1 prophylaxis, while similar guidelines for HIV vaccines remain a key priority. The HIV epidemic continues to cause significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. In 2020, there were approximately 680,000 AIDS-related deaths globally, with young children (aged 0–14 years) accounting for 150,000 new HIV infections, the majority of which occurred during infancy. Existing prevention tools, such as oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), condoms, and medication-assisted treatment for people who inject drugs (PWID), require frequent use, which poses challenges for implementation. New products offering longer durations of protection are expected to have a substantial impact on HIV prevention efforts. For example, the dapivirine vaginal ring (DPR-VR) for women recently received a positive opinion from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) as a monthly prevention option. Additionally, long-acting PrEP with cabotegravir (CAB-LA), administered as a bimonthly injection, demonstrated high effectiveness in preventing HIV infection among cisgender men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender women who have sex with men, and cisgender women in sub-Saharan Africa during the HPTN 083 and HPTN 084 trials. Despite these promising developments, there remains a critical need for interventions that can provide durable or even lifelong protection against HIV infection. WHO and UNAIDS have identified this as a top public health priority. Monoclonal antibodies represent a promising preventative modality due to their ability to target specific epitopes directly. Two parallel Antibody-Mediated Protection (AMP) Phase 2 proof-of-concept efficacy trials recently tested intravenous delivery of the broadly neutralizing antibody (bNAb) VRC01 among women in eastern and southern Africa, as well as among MSM and transgender persons in the Americas. These studies demonstrated that VRC01 was effective in preventing the acquisition of HIV strains sensitive to the antibody but highlighted the need for combinations of antibodies that provide broader and more potent protection. Several more potent combinations and engineered antibodies are currently undergoing early clinical evaluation. However, the HIV vaccine development community has faced recent setbacks. For instance, the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) halted the HVTN 702 clinical trial after interim findings showed that the vaccine did not prevent HIV. Similarly, the Imbokodo study (HVTN 705/HPX2008) found that the vaccine regimen did not provide sufficient protection against HIV infection in young women in sub-Saharan Africa at high risk of acquiring HIV. Nevertheless, several promising vaccine candidates continue to progress into late-stage development. The Phase 3 Mosaico study (HVTN 706) is evaluating an investigational adenovirus-26-based candidate vaccine combined with gp140 protein and mosaic immunogens designed to induce immune responses against a broad array of global HIV strains. Additionally, the PrEPVacc Phase 2b trial, which began enrollment in 2020, is exploring novel approaches to HIV prevention.
